● The research is complete and committed. Here's the digest, organized by your
  seven questions — full depth with equations, constants, and all 204 sources
  lives in research_runs/2026-07-28__auto-skinning-weights/ (synthesis.md for
  cross-referenced conclusions, angles/01–10_*.md for per-topic claims with
  confidence levels and evidence).

  1. Algorithm survey

  Bone heat (Baran & Popović, "Automatic Rigging and Animation of 3D 
  Characters," SIGGRAPH 2007 — Pinocchio). Solves (−Δ + H)wᵢ = Hpᵢ on the
  surface mesh only: cotangent Laplacian, pᵢ = 1 where bone i is nearest, H = 
  c/d² on the diagonal when the vertex-to-bone segment lies inside the volume.
  One sparse factorization, one back-substitution per bone; weights sum to 1 by
  construction. It leaks/fails for two distinct reasons: the
  nearest-visible-bone data term is Euclidean (geometrically close but
  geodesically far surfaces get the wrong seed), and diffusion has nothing
  pulling weights to zero far from bones — Jacobson's SIGGRAPH 2014 course notes
  call locality its weakest property. Blender implements exactly this
  (meshlaplacian.cc, with a BVH ray cast and an undocumented vertex-normal
  cosine term), and its infamous "failed to find solution" error is a singular 
  matrix when any connected component sees no bone — dev-diagnosed in issue
  #45493, a Known Issue since 2015. The published fix in this family is Bone
  Glow (Wareham & Lasenby 2008; exact equations paywalled — flagged, not
  speculated).

  Bounded Biharmonic Weights (Jacobson, Baran, Popović, Sorkine, SIGGRAPH 2011).
  Minimize Σⱼ ½∫‖Δwⱼ‖² over the shape's volume, subject to handle
  interpolation, 0 ≤ w ≤ 1, and partition of unity — a constrained QP per handle
  on a tetrahedral mesh of the interior. Smooth, bounded, shape-aware; the
  quality ceiling among classical methods. Costs: tet meshing (TetGen is fragile
  on real input; fTetWild 2020 fixed robustness but doesn't document conforming
  to interior bone samples), and per-handle QP solves (2011: 3–12 s per handle
  at 50–140k tets; libigl's practical path drops partition-of-unity, solves per
  handle, normalizes after).

  Geodesic Voxel Binding (Dionne & de Lasa, Autodesk, SCA 2013 + TVCG 2014 — 
  Maya's "Geodesic Voxel"). Voxelize by rendering 6 orthographic directions and
  majority-voting interior voxels (this, not ray parity, is what tolerates
  holes/self-intersections/multiple components); Dijkstra-style distance
  propagation per bone through non-exterior voxels; exponential falloff
  max(d_tol,d)^(−λ); truncate to max influences, normalize.
  Geodesic-through-volume beats Euclidean because paths must travel through
  occupied space — a thigh bone can't reach the other leg. Proven on 10/11
  uncleaned internet meshes (one had 660 parts, another 14,982 intersecting
  faces); the 2014 sparse version binds in under ~3 s at 256³. Limits: low
  resolution fuses adjacent limbs; fingers need fine grids; the papers never
  define behavior for geodesically unreachable components (you must pick a
  fallback).

  Delta Mush and post-smoothing. Delta Mush (Mancewicz et al., Rhythm & Hues,
  DigiPro 2014) is a rescue layer, not a weight solver: store rest-pose detail
  as deltas in tangent frames of a Laplacian-smoothed copy; at runtime smooth
  the crudely-skinned mesh and re-add deltas. R&H's primary evidence: every
  character rig since 2010 was a proximity/rigid bind rescued by mush. Direct
  Delta Mush (Le & Lewis, SIGGRAPH 2019) precomputes it into per-vertex-bone 4×4
  matrices (10 floats) plus one 3×3 SVD per vertex — one GPU pass, no
  iteration, with a documented v0–v5 quality ladder (v1 ≡ exact classic DM, v5 ≡
  plain LBS). Plain weight-field smoothing (neighbor averaging + renormalize)
  bakes to zero runtime cost but can only soften transitions — it cannot fix
  wrong-bone assignment.

  Neural skinning (2019→now). NeuroSkinning (2019, NetEase) → RigNet (SIGGRAPH
  2020: joints + hierarchy + weights from a mesh; canonical benchmark) →
  HeterSkinNet/SkinningNet/Neural Blend Shapes/TARig → the 2024–25
  autoregressive wave (Make-It-Animatable ~0.5 s/character; UniRig, SIGGRAPH
  2025, MIT code; MagicArticulate, Apache-2.0). Production-viability verdict:
  quality gains are real on-distribution (RigNet's deformation error beats GVB
  and BBW on its benchmark), but everything hinges on training distribution —
  RigNet needs 1K–5K-vertex remeshes and its repo is GPLv3-or-commercial with a
  legally murky dataset; the 2025 models' checkpoints were trained on
  Objaverse-derived data of untested provenance. No DCC or engine publicly
  documents cross-character neural weight prediction in production; what shipped
  (Unreal's ML Deformer, ZivaRT) is per-character deformation approximation, a
  different problem.

  3. Hard cases

  - Separate pieces (clothing, hair, sockets): voxel binding bridges components
  (all meshes voxelized as one solid — documented Maya behavior); surface heat
  strands them (and in Blender one stranded island kills the whole solve). The
  dedicated tool is "Robust Skin Weights Transfer via Weight Inpainting" 
  (Abdrashitov, Raichstat, Monsen, Hill — Epic Games, SIGGRAPH Asia 2023): copy
  body weights where closest-point matches pass gates (distance ≤ 0.05·bbox
  diagonal, normals within 35°), biharmonically inpaint the rest, flipped-normal
  pass for inner layers. MIT reference code; core is ~40 lines. Known gap:
  fully disconnected garment islands with zero confident matches.
  - Holes/non-manifold: voxel voting shrugs it off; heat needs
  weld/degenerate-cleanup first; BBW needs fTetWild-class meshing (or the 2024
  mesh-free biharmonic — Dodik et al., arXiv 2406.00238 — which runs on soup).
  - Under 1000 triangles: an evidence desert — no paper evaluates it.
  Practitioner norm is rigid per-joint assignment (smooth falloff quantizes to
  steps at that density anyway); learned methods are out of their envelope. The
  angle file labels this the weakest-sourced case.
  - Non-human proportions: the geometric solvers (heat/voxel/BBW) are
  proportion-agnostic given a placed skeleton — Pinocchio's weights drove a
  rigged donut. Humanoid assumptions live in skeleton-fitting (Pinocchio
  embedding penalizes off-template proportions) and learned methods (Mixamo:
  bipeds only, "wings and tails may not work").

  4. Semantic heuristics — the headline finding

  The premise is confirmed by patent, not folklore. Mixamo's US 8,797,328 B2
  describes: build a closed proxy mesh from the dirty multi-part upload → detect
  salient points (or take the user's markers) → fit a template skeleton with
  statistical priors, deliberately inserting clavicle/mid-foot joints because 
  they're "useful in the skinning" → solve weights segment-wise by heat
  diffusion with "problem specific diffusion coefficients and Dirichlet-type 
  boundary conditions… estimated using machine learning… skinning templates that
  are specific for a given joint" → transfer back via mean-value coordinates.
  That is literally a "shoulder-aware" strategy: per-joint learned solve
  parameters plus helper-joint insertion, layered over a generic core. A second
  patent (US 9,305,387) shows the other regime: where Mixamo controls topology,
  it doesn't solve at all — it copies artist weights from rigged templates.
  AccuRIG documents classification-before-weighting (cloth → smooth solve;
  helmets/armor → rigid auto-attach to a neighboring bone) and claims per-limb
  optimized weights, but its solver is a total black box (no whitepaper, no
  patents found). Caveat kept explicit throughout: patents show 2010–2014
  intent, not necessarily today's shipped code.

  5. Joint placement

  Three families: template embedding (Pinocchio's other half — medial-surface
  sphere packing, graph construction, A*-style discrete search over 9 learned
  penalty functions; 13/16 success, fails on off-template proportions, and its
  authors admit no reliable geometric way to place knees/elbows); geometric 
  skeletonization (Au et al. mesh contraction, SIGGRAPH 2008; Tagliasacchi's
  mean-curvature skeletons, shipped as a two-call CGAL API — but a curve
  skeleton has no joint semantics, and conversion to an animation skeleton is
  folklore); learned/landmark (RigNet's displace-then-cluster joint prediction;
  Mixamo's ~8 user markers; SMPL fitting for human scans; 2025 autoregressive
  skeleton generators). For a tool where users build arbitrary creatures, the
  defensible stack is user-guided markers + template fit first, CGAL skeleton as
  an assist, learned as optional.

  7. Validation

  Academic standard trio (RigNet/SkinningNet/NeuroSkinning): precision/recall of
  influential-bone sets (threshold 1e-4), average L1 between weight vectors,
  and deformation error under sampled poses — with SkinningNet stating outright
  the first two "are not good enough"; trust deformation error. Without ground
  truth: glTF-spec structural rules (non-negative MUST, sum≈1, influence caps
  4/8/12 per engine docs, no zero-weight vertices, no NaN); per-bone
  influence-island connectivity + geodesic-radius outliers (catches sleeve→torso
  leakage — my synthesis, motivated by the GVB and inpainting papers); pose
  sweeps at 90–180° (papers only test ±10° — too gentle) tracking
  divergence-theorem volume ratio, per-edge stretch spikes (localizes
  armpit/crotch boundary bugs, grounded in Epic's crease observation), and
  self-intersection counts. Crucially: candy-wrapper and volume collapse are
  intrinsic LBS artifacts (Lewis et al. 2000; DQS is the mitigation) — the
  validator should run each sweep under LBS and DQS with identical weights; only
  artifacts persisting under both are weight bugs. No studio publishes a
  thresholded skin-QA suite; all absolute thresholds are project-tuned
  constants.

  ---
  Corrections the research surfaced against common belief: the weight-inpainting
  paper is Epic Games, not Roblox; Unreal's Deformer Graph sample is classic
  iterative Delta Mush, not DDM; Pinocchio's library is LGPL, not MIT; and GVB's
  own two papers contradict each other on voxel connectivity (6- vs
  26-connected — use 6-connected per the 2013 text).

  Repo state: committed as b76f5711f, req_3487 moved to review, and a memory

  auto-skinning built into the editor, the evidence-backed shape is in
  synthesis.md under "Recommended Stack" — voxel-geodesic core in the framework,
  rigid-attach + inpainting for our multi-part models, mush rescue, pose-sweep
  validator.

● Phase 1 is built, verified, and committed (b1897782b) — the framework now has
  a real skinned-figure path. Here's where things stand:

  What landed. The player can now render as one palette-blended skinned mesh
  instead of N separate part draws. The whole chain is in place: a skinned WGSL
  shader (assembled from the same shared chunks as the standard mesh shader, so
  the lighting/fog/wireframe/shadow behavior is identical by construction), a
  28-byte skinned vertex format carrying bone indices + weights, a per-figure
  bone-palette storage buffer, matching shadow-pass support, a new
  __compiled_world_set_player_skin door, and per-frame palette updates driven by
  the exact same clip sampler and webcam live-pose feed that pose the body
  today.

  Why you won't see anything change yet — by design. The editor currently
  exports rigid weights (every vertex 100% its own part), and the palette math
  mirrors the existing per-part transform math exactly. So the skinned path
  reproduces today's look — that's the parity proof that the substrate is
  correct. The interesting part comes next: the Phase-2 voxel-geodesic solver
  writes soft weights into this same wire format, and seams start deforming
  smoothly instead of hinging.

  Verified: the editor cart compiles clean, and rjit shot editor --route /play
  passes — world, UI, and the player figure all render headless (screenshots in
  the session scratchpad). One honest caveat: the shot harness doesn't surface
  the loader's log line, so I couldn't confirm from the capture alone whether
  the headless boot's figure went through the skin door or the stand-in path —
  your next rjit dev/playtest run will say [loader] player skin from live push —
  N verts × M bones (SKIN-3499) in the console when the skinned path is live.
  If anything ever looks off, the legacy per-part path is fully intact — it's

● Green light received — this is slice 2 of the same arc (req_3499): the
  voxel-geodesic auto-weight solver in Zig. The design, straight from the
  research: rasterize the body into a voxel grid with multi-axis parity voting
  (junk-tolerant), seed each bone's distance field from its own part's surface
  voxels (the Lego part structure is the prior), Dijkstra through the interior
  with the armpit-fixing boundary penalty, exponential falloff to top-4 weights,
  then a light weld-aware smoothing pass. It runs host-side when the skin
  payload is staged, rewriting the rigid weights in place — zero wire changes.

● The webcam agent is done, and it found the smoking gun — reproduced it 
  standalone, not just theorized. You were right that it wasn't a device quirk:
  every camera hit the same wall.

  The root cause. framework/render/render_surfaces.zig tore down the camera's
  ffmpeg child by calling std.process.Child.kill on the frame thread. In Zig
  0.16 that call is one SIGTERM followed by an uncancelable blocking wait. But
  ffmpeg at that moment is blocked mid-write, pushing a 3.6MB raw frame into a
  64KB pipe that just stopped being drained — and its signal handlers
  auto-restart the write, so that single SIGTERM never lands. ffmpeg never
  exits, the frame thread waits on it forever, and the whole app is frozen. The
  extra cruelty: SDL converts a kill you send into a quit event that only that
  frozen thread could process — which is exactly why plain kill did nothing and
  kill -9 was the only way out. Every teardown path funnels there — switching
  cameras, leaving the tab, quitting — with any camera, which matches your
  experience precisely. The agent found the same landmine in the qemu,
  app-window, and Xvfb child teardowns and fixed all of them.

  The fix (commit 15368781b, reqs 3503/3504 in review). A new
  framework/render/child_teardown.zig: the frame thread never waits on a child
  again — hard-kill immediately, reap on a detached background task that
  shutdown cancels rather than awaits. Plus quality-of-life it added while in
  there: a camera that opens but never streams now fails loudly after 10 seconds
  ("is the camera streaming? (OBS: Start Virtual Camera)") instead of showing
  an eternal black square, and it auto-retries every 10s so it heals itself the
  moment you hit Start Virtual Camera; ffmpeg errors now print their reason; and
  pose inference can no longer read uninitialized frame bytes.

  Proof so far: a standalone test reproduces your exact freeze state — a
  SIGTERM-immune child blocked on a full pipe — and shows the old code hangs
  forever while the new teardown completes in under 2 seconds. All capture tests
  pass, the editor ships clean, headless shot passes. Honest limit: no camera
  exists on this box, so the final live proof is yours.
